section_title: Mercy and the Lord of the Sabbath

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. 2 When the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.” 3 Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? 4 He entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests.

5 Or haven’t you read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent? 6 But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here. 7 If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. 8 For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

context_lines: The disciples are hungry and pick grain as they walk through a field. The objection concerns doing this on the Sabbath. [Deuteronomy 23:24–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/23.htm) permits eating from a neighbor's vineyard or plucking grain by hand while forbidding taking a supply away in a basket or harvesting with a sickle. The dispute here concerns the day, rather than simply taking someone else's food.

Jesus answers from Scripture. First He recalls David receiving consecrated bread when he and his companions were hungry ([1 Samuel 21:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_samuel/21.htm)). Jesus explicitly says that this bread was lawful only for priests. [Leviticus 24:5–9](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/24.htm) assigns it to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place. The example asks His hearers to reckon with human need, rather than treating David as an obvious ground for condemnation.

Then He points to priests serving in the temple on the Sabbath. The Law itself requires Sabbath offerings ([Numbers 28:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/28.htm)). Their service involves work, yet they are innocent. Jesus brings the comparison to Himself: One greater than the temple is present, and the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

His quotation from [Hosea 6:6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hosea/6.htm) puts mercy at the heart of the response. The Greek word is ἔλεος, *eleos* (EH-leh-oss), mercy or compassion expressed toward people in need. [Thayer's entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/1656.htm) includes this verse and the readiness to help those in trouble. Knowing what God desires should have kept the critics from condemning the innocent.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as joining Jesus' authority over the Sabbath with God's concern for mercy and human need. [Wesley on Matthew 12:3–8](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) emphasizes need, the priority of mercy, and the disciples serving under Jesus' authority. The Catholic [Catechism, 582](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P1N.HTM), teaches that serving God and neighbor does not violate Sabbath rest. The Reformed [Westminster Confession, 21.8](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), also includes duties of necessity and mercy within faithful Sabbath observance. The shared point here is that compassion belongs within honoring God.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The claim to be greater than the temple points toward Jesus' central place in bringing people to God. In [John 2:18–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/2.htm), He speaks of the temple being destroyed and raised, and John explains that He means His body. He points to His own death and resurrection as the greater reality behind the temple.

[Ephesians 2:18–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm) develops that wider picture: through Christ, people have access to the Father by the Spirit, and together become God's dwelling place. This is a connection across the New Testament, rather than a claim that Matthew explains every part of it here. Jesus' authority is bound to the greater work of bringing people near to God.
